title: Tesla's Momentum Can't Be Stopped - Lifeboat News: The Blog
content:
Tesla’s latest blog outlines the company’s continued momentum in the electric‑vehicle market, highlighting several key developments.  The robo‑taxi service in California now operates until 2 a.m. with only four hours of downtime, a change that the company says demonstrates operational readiness and confidence in the system’s performance.  To support global expansion, Tesla is hiring a senior software engineer in Fremont to build backend systems for real‑time pricing and fees, and it is recruiting autopilot data‑collection supervisors for night and afternoon shifts in Arizona, Florida, Texas and Nevada.  The company also plans to use surge pricing during high‑demand events such as the Super Bowl, while aiming to keep fares lower than competitors.  Tesla’s robo‑taxis will employ ultra‑wideband, Bluetooth low energy and Wi‑Fi for context‑aware interactions, enabling features like pre‑ordering drinks and automated transactions.

In the realm of Full Self‑Driving (FSD), Tesla’s version 14 boasts a 10‑fold increase in parameter count, which the company claims will improve resolution for driving decisions and ride comfort.  The AI‑enhanced vision cameras can now detect drowsy drivers, lane departure and obstacles in real time, and the system can simulate future scenarios based on millions of past videos, reportedly allowing it to “see 20 miles down the street.”  FSD’s object recognition has become crisper, identifying mailboxes, curbs and cars to aid in complex parking and situational awareness.  The system can also assist impaired drivers by applying emergency control when necessary, a feature noted by former C‑Level executive Jeff Lutz.

Tesla’s long‑term strategy includes a software‑update plan that will keep vehicles up to 12 years old receiving performance improvements.  The company’s patents for improved FSD visualizations and backend pricing systems further support its robo‑taxi platform.  "Tesla’s robo‑taxi service now operates until 2 a.m. with only 4 hours of downtime," the blog notes, underscoring the company’s confidence in its readiness for expanded service.

Overall, the article presents Tesla’s technological innovations and expansion plans in a factual, data‑driven manner, with no overt bias or sensationalism.

title: 特斯拉自动驾驶出租车上线首日爆红，但规模化落地仍需考验
content: Tesla’s newly launched autonomous ride‑hailing service sparked a viral craze on its first day, with download figures reportedly exceeding industry expectations and reaching up to six times the volume of some leading competitors, according to the article.  The service is currently available only in Austin, Texas, and the Bay Area, and it supports only iPhone users; Android users must wait for a future release, a point that has drawn criticism from some users who question why such restrictions persist in 2025.  Tesla responded that the Android version is under accelerated development.  In the past two months, the company logged only one safety incident, and overall passenger feedback has been largely positive.  However, every vehicle still carries a safety driver, and Elon Musk has pledged to eliminate this human oversight by the end of the year.  Industry experts caution that high download numbers do not equate to operational capacity; the current user base mainly consists of early testers who queued for the service.  To achieve true scale, Tesla must address vehicle deployment volumes, regulatory approvals, pricing, safety, and reliability.  The article concludes that while public enthusiasm for cutting‑edge technology is high, sustained success in autonomous ride‑hailing will require more than traffic and buzz.

title: Tesla Robotaxi Gains Approval in Arizona, Expanding U.S. Footprint - TechStory
content: Tesla has secured approval to operate its Robotaxi service in Arizona, making it the fourth U.S. state to allow the company to test and run autonomous ride‑hailing vehicles. The company announced the decision late Friday, following earlier approvals in Austin, Texas (June 2023), California (Bay Area) and Nevada (earlier this month). CEO Elon Musk has stated that Tesla’s long‑term goal is to provide Robotaxi rides to half of the U.S. population, with nationwide coverage as the ultimate objective. In Arizona, the approval requires ‘Safety Drivers,’ a term that suggests Tesla‑trained personnel will oversee operations, though the exact seating arrangement remains unclear. The state’s acceptance follows a history of autonomous vehicle pilots by companies such as Waymo and Cruise, positioning Arizona as a favorable testing ground. Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet has expanded since its Austin debut, with demand increasing after the service opened to a broader public user base. Despite the recent approvals, regulatory approval remains the biggest bottleneck, as state‑level rules for driverless ride‑hailing are still evolving. With four states now permitting the service, Tesla is laying the groundwork for a multi‑state Robotaxi network, though the transition from pilot programs to full commercial operations will depend on continued regulatory support.

title: Tesla veut des millions de robotaxis d'ici 2025, mais Waymo gagnera-t-il le jeu à long terme ? | Invezz FR
content: Tesla and Waymo are racing to dominate the autonomous ride‑hailing market, taking very different deployment paths. After launching its first robotaxi test in Austin in June 2024, Tesla CEO Elon Musk told investors that driverless Teslas could serve ‘la moitié de la population des États-Unis’ by the end of 2024, a claim that would cover roughly 50 % of the U.S. population. Waymo, owned by Alphabet, has been testing commercial autonomous services for over eight years but now operates only in zones that represent about 3 % of the U.S. population. The two companies differ in technology and strategy: Tesla relies on cameras and AI to scale quickly without detailed mapping, while Waymo uses high‑definition maps, LIDAR and a step‑by‑step AI process to prioritize safety. Tesla’s goal is to have ‘des millions de Teslas fonctionnant de manière autonome’ by the second half of 2025, whereas Waymo’s 2023 financials show a loss of between 1.2 and 1.5 billion dollars, though analysts expect profitability as costs fall and ridership rises. Safety incidents have highlighted regulatory challenges: Waymo vehicles in Austin have been cited three times since March for failing to respond to manual signals, and one vehicle crashed into floodwater in May; Tesla’s fleet is still in early stages with limited interactions. Regulatory and community engagement also diverge: Waymo has built long‑term relationships with local groups in Austin, while Tesla informed school officials only shortly before launch. Morningstar predicts Tesla’s robotaxis may not be fully deployed until 2028 but could overtake Waymo’s market share by the end of the decade. The competition underscores how rapid expansion versus cautious rollout can shape the future of autonomous ride‑hailing.

title: Robotaxi Tesla: da settembre servizio accessibile al pubblico
content: Tesla is set to take a major step forward in its vision for the future of mobility. The company has announced that its Robotaxi service, which has been available by invitation only, will be made available to the public starting from September 2025. The service, which uses Tesla Model Y vehicles equipped with autonomous driving technology, will allow anyone to book a ride. This marks an important milestone in Tesla's strategy, which has been focused on autonomous transportation for years. The announcement comes at a crucial time, as Tesla has just received the official license for ride-sharing in Texas, putting it alongside giants like Uber, Lyft, and Waymo. The public Robotaxi service will debut in Austin, where Tesla has already tested the system in real-world conditions. For now, a human operator will be present in the passenger seat, ready to intervene in case of emergencies. This is a significant step towards full autonomy, but human intervention will still be necessary. In other states, where Tesla has launched more limited forms of ride-hailing, a human driver is still required, although the vehicle can use Full Self Driving Supervised technology. The expansion of the service to other cities will be gradual, but the goal is clear: to deploy a large-scale network of driverless transportation. The opening to the public in Austin is just the first step.

title: Tesla Robotaxi makes major expansion with official public app launch
content: Tesla announced that its Robotaxi suite is now publicly available, launching a dedicated iOS app that puts users on a waitlist to ride driverless Model Y vehicles. The program, which began in Austin in late June, has expanded over ten weeks to a 190‑square‑mile geofence that now includes Giga Texas, Austin‑Bergstrom International Airport, and freeway driving. Tesla has also moved the safety monitor to the driver’s seat on freeways. The expansion signals Tesla’s confidence to open the service to more riders beyond the initial private beta. According to the article, the app launch marks a major achievement for Tesla, as the company is "confident to begin allowing more riders to utilize the platform". It also notes that "Once you download the app, you will be put on a waitlist to enter the company's list of riders." The Robotaxi program has been active for two and a half months, with nearly three months of operation and a fleet that has grown over the past ten weeks.

title: Tesla FSD turns off more U.S. consumers than its attracts, survey finds
content: A new survey by Slingshot Strategies found that 35% of 8,000 U.S. respondents said Tesla’s Full Self‑Driving (FSD) would make them less likely to buy a Tesla, while only 14% said it would make them more likely; the remaining 51% said it would have no effect. Nearly half of respondents believe FSD technology should be illegal. The findings come amid a sales slump for Tesla, with European sales falling 40% in July year‑over‑year and increased competition from rivals such as Waymo and Baidu’s Apollo Go. Tesla is also testing a ride‑hailing service in Austin and San Francisco, with human supervisors in Austin and drivers at the wheel in San Francisco. Elon Musk, who has said the future of Tesla depends on autonomous vehicles, recently stated that a new Model Y variant “won’t start production in the U.S. until the end of next year” and “might not ever, given the advent of self‑driving in America.”

title: 2025 Tesla Model Y Robotaxi First Ride Review: Smooth, but glitchy
content: Tesla’s first autonomous ride‑hailing test in Austin, Texas, involved seven Model Y Robotaxi rides. The vehicles ran with a safety monitor in the passenger seat and required an invitation to use the service, limiting early users to Tesla employees, press and influencers. The Robotaxi app linked to the rider’s Tesla account and allowed one adult guest. Rides operated only between 6 a.m. and 12 p.m. and were restricted to a geofenced area; the service did not serve the airport terminal. The first trip, requested at 3:39 p.m., promised a 15‑minute ride for $6.90, compared with Lyft’s $10.67 for 14 minutes and UberX’s $11.91 for 15 minutes. The vehicle arrived 20 yards away, and a yellow bar appeared on the rear screen stating, 'Our team has identified an issue and is working to resolve it.' A voice from headquarters acknowledged the problem. The car accelerated smoothly, but the driver’s monitor noted that the vehicle ran 5‑7 mph above the posted 35‑mph limit on wide streets and stopped at a green light when the crosswalk was clear. The ride ended at the wrong hotel, and the app prompted the driver to exit safely. Subsequent rides repeated similar issues, including a fault that triggered emergency flashers during a left turn. The reviewer concluded that while the cabin was comfortable and the driving smooth, the Robotaxi’s safety glitches and lack of full‑autonomous capability raised concerns about releasing Full Self‑Driving unsupervised. The article compares Tesla’s cameras‑only approach to Waymo’s lidar‑radar system, noting that Tesla’s vehicles may struggle in adverse weather.

title: Tesla Robotaxi App on iOS Is Now Available to Download, But There's a Waitlist
content: Tesla has released its Robotaxi app on iOS, enabling U.S. users of legal age to register and join the autonomous ride‑hailing service that is currently being tested in Austin, Texas, and San Francisco, California. The public launch marks the first time the service moves beyond early access, but a waitlist still applies. Engadget reports that in a Business Insider test a user waited only three hours before being able to start a ride, though wait times may vary. In Austin the service uses Cybercab electric vehicles, while San Francisco customers can book regular Tesla EVs. The app lets users change pickup points, view estimated fare, arrival time and trip duration, and, once a ride is booked, press 'Start' to begin. During the trip passengers can adjust cabin temperature, seat position and stream music via the in‑vehicle touchscreen. The announcement came from Tesla’s verified account on X and was covered by Tech Times on September 5 2025.

title: Tesla starts Full Self-Driving rollout to owners in Australia
content: Tesla has begun rolling out its Full Self‑Driving (Supervised) suite to owners in Australia, following the official launch of the driver‑assist package in the country on 28 August 2025. The rollout will start with Hardware 4‑equipped Model 3 and Model Y vehicles and will proceed in stages, with the first stage already underway. Tesla cautions drivers that the system is not fully autonomous and requires the driver to remain attentive. The suite is currently sold outright for $10,100, with a subscription model under development. Australia is the sixth country to receive the FSD (Supervised) package, after the United States, Canada, Mexico, China and Puerto Rico. In China the feature is marketed as “City Autopilot” due to regulatory differences. Early reviews are positive; a journalist remarked, 'To have this car drive me around Brisbane for an hour, we're talking in the city, motorway, spaghetti bowl of on‑ramps, it handled it so well. It was mind‑blowing.'
